answers.answer: Caching could avoid repeated 80 ms guide-building reads for the frequently reused station-language pairs; a usable hit needs the 2 ms cache lookup instead. Weekly changes make reuse promising, but the team still needs to decide acceptable staleness and how to remove outdated guides. Use station-guide:{stationId}:{language}, because language changes the answer. On a hit the API application looks up that key and returns its stored guide; a hit can still be stale. On a miss the API application reads/builds the guide from the authoritative database, writes the result under that key in the cache, and returns it. The cache does not fetch it itself. A miss still pays the database work plus the cache lookup and cache write; no total miss latency is established because cache-write time is unspecified. Caching also adds storage and operations to keep copies current. Losing the cached guide does not lose the database record.

evidence.quote: The API checks and fills the cache explicitly. The cache does not fetch the result from the database on its own.
Include the inputs that change the answer.
The application finds a usable entry under the requested key and returns the stored result.
No usable entry exists. The application reads the database, stores a copy in the cache and returns the result.
Creating the copy still costs work: fetch or compute the result, then write it to the cache. Storage, lookups and keeping copies current all have costs.

answers.answer: C receives the old hours. A fetched the old database value before B committed; deleting the key at step 3 does not stop A from storing its already-fetched old value at step 4. C then hits that newly stored stale entry. The team cannot claim every read after B finishes sees the new hours. For this freshness-critical endpoint, a simple way to avoid this cached copy is for each reader to read the authoritative database directly instead of serving the cache. Under the supplied commit prerequisite, C reading the database after B commits sees the new hours. The lesson does not specify a concurrency protocol for making cache fills and writes consistent, and none is needed for that bypass.

evidence.quote: Saving the price and removing the copy are separate steps. A reader can fetch $20 before the update, pause, then refill $20 after removal. The next cache hit still returns $20. Removal can also fail.
Keep freshness-critical decisions tied to authoritative data.

answers.answer: Case A: at 12:03 the original entry has not expired, so the request can hit it and receive the old forecast despite the 12:02 source change. At 12:11 it has expired, so the request must fetch the source and can store a new copy. Case B: at 12:05 the original entry has already been removed for memory, so the request must fetch the source even though the original ten-minute lifetime would not have ended until 12:10. The TTL limits how long that entry may remain before expiration; it does not schedule a refresh, promise the value reflects source changes, or guarantee it will stay present for ten minutes. It limits entry lifetime rather than the age of source data used to fill it. The 12:04 removal is eviction to make room, distinct from time-based expiration.

evidence.quote: Sets how long an entry may remain before it expires. A 60-second TTL does not refresh the data every minute; a later miss must load it again.
Removes entries to make room.
An entry can be evicted before its TTL ends.
TTL limits an entry's lifetime, not the age of the source data used to fill it.

answers.answer: One shared cache is the simpler fit for one deletion to remove the map used by every instance, given the accepted network lookup and the stated single entry/no concurrent fills assumption. Today each local lookup happens inside the receiving API process. Deleting the writer instance's copy leaves the other three copies present; requests routed to those instances can hit their old maps. A request to the cleared instance misses and reloads the database. With a shared cache, each API instance makes a network call to the separate cache service for the same entry. Deleting that entry removes the common cached map, so a later miss reloads the database. The shared service adds a network call and operating cost, and does not itself ensure future database changes are reflected without an update policy. Losing one local cache affects only its own instance; the other instances keep theirs. An unreachable shared cache prevents all four instances from accessing its entries.

evidence.quote: Lives inside each API process. Reads avoid a network call, but each process fills and updates its own copy. Their copies can reflect different versions of the same data.
Several API servers use a separate cache service, such as Redis or Memcached. They can reuse entries, but each lookup adds a network call and the service needs operating.
Restarting one API process discards its local cache; other processes keep their copies. If the shared cache is unreachable, every API server using it loses access to those cached entries.
Sharing reduces separate copies. It does not automatically keep the cache current with the database.

answers.answer: When the popular key expires, many simultaneous misses can independently read the same schedule from the database and exceed its safe 500 reads/second. Have the application coalesce those misses: one reader starts the database lookup while concurrent readers share that in-progress lookup and its result, then the result fills the cache. That replaces many duplicate reads for the same schedule with one shared read. The lesson gives the behavior, not the mechanism for coordinating it across application instances. During a full outage, sending all 10,000 requests/second to the database would exceed the safe rate by a factor of 20. Bound total fallback schedule reads across the service to at most the safe 500/second and return temporary errors for excess requests; rejecting them avoids their database work. If a last-known schedule remains accessible outside the unreachable cache and is within the permitted 60-second staleness window, serve it to more callers without database reads. Do not assume an unreachable cache can supply that old value, or serve it past the permitted window. The question does not establish that a separately accessible old copy exists, so bounded fallback plus errors is the response that works without that assumption. Test the empty/unavailable-cache case to check that protection holds.

evidence.quote: Many requests miss the same key together and repeat its database lookup. Coalescing requests lets concurrent readers share one in-progress lookup.

A cache outage can turn most reads into database traffic. Limit fallback work to what the database can handle; reject excess requests or serve older data only where the application permits stale results.
Test with an empty or unavailable cache. A warm cache can hide insufficient database capacity.

answers.answer: Do not add this cache now. Each result is read exactly once, so writing it to a cache after that read creates no future hit and avoids no database read. The current 2 ms database read is small compared with the 100 ms endpoint budget, and ten reads/second is comfortably within the stated database capacity. That does not establish total endpoint latency, but there is no demonstrated reuse or database-load benefit here. Filling the cache still adds write work and storage; checking it adds lookups, and maintaining copies adds management costs. Reconsider if the same inspection results begin receiving frequent repeated reads, especially if obtaining them becomes expensive or database load rises enough that avoiding those reads helps. Then measure response time, database load, hit ratio and miss costs, and decide acceptable staleness.

evidence.quote: If requests rarely reuse results, or freshness is too hard to maintain, the cache may cost more than it saves.
Creating the copy still costs work: fetch or compute the result, then write it to the cache. Storage, lookups and keeping copies current all have costs.
Choose results that are expensive enough to obtain, frequently reused and able to tolerate a defined amount of staleness.
Compare response time and database load before and after caching. Track hit ratio, the fraction of lookups served from the cache, and the cost of misses.
